posts.text:
We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Read more on our new Safeguards blog:
posts.why_viral: New self-monitoring safety technique that scales with model capability
posts.why_it_matters: Practical safeguard for production agent deployments

posts.text:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.
posts.why_viral: Detailed post-incident report on real monitoring systems that caught breakouts
posts.why_it_matters: Concrete techniques for monitoring autonomous agents in production

posts.text:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog:
posts.why_viral: Agents inventing subtle misalignment data that fools monitors
posts.why_it_matters: Shows scalable automated red-teaming for training data filters

posts.text:
Software is not dead. Here's my unfiltered, honest opinion about using AI for SWE, even in highly complex domains.

It's true that AI is good. Like really good. You can open a complex project in C++, give your Claude Code agent a JIRA task and ask it to create an implementation plan. And it will "almost" work.

As in 95% of it will be correct. So you can literally be a dumb sloperator who just executes commands. But in the remaining 5% it truly matters.

AI can educate you about trade-offs. It can't decide for you. You have to learn that decision-making skill.

quoted_post.text:
Software is dead

It's now the era of personal software and everyone just builds what they need whenever they need it I think

posts.why_viral: Nuanced counter to "software is dead" with specific 95% experience
posts.why_it_matters: Practical reminder that judgment and trade-off decisions still matter

posts.text:
Claude Code and Codex can push dozens of PRs a day now. Writing the code takes minutes, and the rest of the time goes to waiting on CI, the checks and tests GitHub runs every time you push.

Nine changes took each PR's CI 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗼 𝟰𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝟮. One step was having an agent pull the last 150 CI runs and split every job into three parts: waiting for a machine, setup, and actually running. That alone showed that half the test jobs 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻'𝘁 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲 at all, a bug that had been sitting there for a whole year.

Send this prompt to Claude Code or Codex to find out where your CI time goes, then cut it down one piece at a time 👇

"Audit this repo's CI:
1. Use gh to pull the last 150 CI runs and split each job's time into three parts: waiting in the queue for a machine, setup (checkout, installing dependencies, restoring the cache), and actually running the task. List the 5 slowest jobs and how many seconds each part takes.
2. Check these 9 things one by one: queueing on the default runners; slow lint; slow typechecking; tests that aren't sharded, or machines that are too small; every test file reloading the whole app; slow setup (cache misses, clones that aren't blobless, more parallel tasks than cores); jobs that don't run in parallel; every PR running the full test suite; no local checks before push.
3. For each problem, tell me how many seconds it costs now, which line of which file to change, and roughly how much it would save. List the ones that cost more money (new runners, bigger machines) or run fewer tests separately for me to decide.
Give me the report first. Don't change anything."
posts.why_viral: Ready-to-paste prompt that cut CI from 40 min to 2 min with concrete results
posts.why_it_matters: Immediate actionable workflow for any team using coding agents
